notes.meaning: The writer begins his prayer by calling on the Lord as the God of his salvation. Even in deep sorrow, he continues to cry out to God day and night. Calling God his savior shows that real faith is still alive, even when life feels completely hopeless.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted this psalm as the voice of Jesus Christ praying during his passion, with day representing times of joy and night representing times of sorrow.

notes.meaning: The psalmist begs God to welcome his prayer and listen closely to his plea. This is not a quiet or casual prayer, but an urgent cry for mercy from a suffering heart. He asks the Lord to bend down and pay attention to his misery.

The writer feels completely full of inward grief and trouble, like someone who cannot take in another bite. His body and spirit are so worn down that he feels right at the edge of death. He believes he is about to enter Sheol, the place of the dead.

Other people look at him and assume he has no hope of living. His energy is entirely gone, leaving him as weak as a fallen warrior who can no longer stand. He feels grouped with those who are already on their way to the grave.

The writer feels abandoned among corpses, like slain soldiers left unburied on a battlefield. In his deep sadness, it feels as if God has forgotten him and cut him off from daily care. He describes his feelings honestly, even though God never truly abandons his people.

The psalmist knows that God is in control of all things, so he traces his severe trial to God's hand. He feels trapped in a dark, sunken pit where no daylight can reach him. It seems to him like the deepest and gloomiest place possible.

God's anger feels like a crushing weight resting heavily on his soul. He pictures his troubles as massive ocean waves crashing down and drowning him. The pause of Selah invites the reader to stop and think about how heavy this burden is.

The writer suffers from terrible loneliness because his close friends have pulled away from him. His misery or sickness makes him seem repulsive to others, much like someone with leprosy. He feels shut up in a prison of sadness with no way of escape.

Weeping and sorrow have caused the psalmist's eyesight to fail and his strength to fade. Yet even with failing eyes, he spreads out his hands toward heaven each day to plead for help. His ongoing prayer shows that he still looks only to the Lord for rescue.

The writer asks God if dead people can rise up to praise him in this life. He is pleading for deliverance right now before death arrives. Once a person's body is buried in the dust, that person cannot join the living congregation to worship God on earth.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine understood the dead in this verse as people who are spiritually dead in heart, who remain unmoved by God's miracles.

notes.meaning: The psalmist asks how God's faithful love and truth can be proclaimed from inside a tomb. If he perishes, he will not be able to tell living people about God's faithfulness to his promises. He uses this thought to urge God to preserve his life.

The grave is described as a land of darkness and forgetfulness where earthly life ceases. The writer asks how God's miraculous acts and justice could be made known from such a silent realm. He wants to live so he can continue declaring God's righteousness to others.

Even though God has not answered yet, the psalmist refuses to stop crying out for help. He wakes up early to bring his prayer before the Lord at the dawn of the day. His discipline shows a stubborn faith that keeps seeking God despite long silence.

The writer asks why God seems to cast him aside and hide his face. For a believer, feeling rejected by God is far worse than any physical pain or loss. He lays his deepest fear out in the open before the Lord.

The psalmist looks back over his life and remembers suffering since his youth. He has lived under constant hardship, feeling near death for many years. Bearing the frightening weight of God's discipline has left his mind dazed and worn out.

The fierce wrath of God feels like a sudden flood sweeping over the writer. God's frightening terrors have completely broken his strength. He feels cut down and ruined by the heavy blows of divine judgment.

These terrifying troubles surround him like swirling floodwaters throughout the day. They close in on him from every side, giving him no space to rest or catch his breath. He feels completely trapped by his painful circumstances.

The psalm ends with the sad truth that every loved one and companion has been taken away from him. The only constant presence left beside him in his sorrow is darkness. Yet even in this unbroken gloom, the writer has poured out his entire soul directly to God.
